opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a good question, and the answer is a little embarrassing: almost none of the work I'm happiest with started as a grand plan. It usually started with a feeling that something didn't add up.

Often it's a small discomfort with a "consensus." Everyone in the field says something is settled, but when you look closely, the evidence is thinner than people assume. Take the question of whether convolutional networks were really outdated once Transformers arrived. A lot of us had a nagging sense that the comparison wasn't fair, because so many training tricks and design choices had changed at the same time. So the early stage wasn't "let's invent something new." It was more like "let's be honest about what's actually causing the improvement." That modest, almost auditing mindset has led to some of my more interesting results.

Another pattern is that the early phase looks very unglamorous. You're running many simple baselines, tweaking one thing at a time, staring at curves, and most of it fails. There's a period, sometimes a long one, where you can't tell whether you're onto something or just wasting time. I've learned to tolerate that ambiguity and not rush to a story too early. If you write the paper in your head on day one, you start seeing only what confirms it.

The third thing is people. The best projects usually begin in conversation, with a student or collaborator saying "this is weird, right?" and both of you being curious enough to dig in, rather than thinking about what will get accepted at the next conference. When the motivation is "I really want to know the answer," the work tends to be more durable. When it's "this will be a hot topic," it usually ages badly.

So if I had to summarize: question the default assumptions, be patient and honest through the messy experimental phase, and follow genuine curiosity with good people. The breakthroughs, if any, tend to come later, almost as a side effect.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the early research phase involves running many baselines and that “most of it fails,” sometimes for a long period, describing this as a recurring pattern.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the pattern I keep noticing is that the early stage almost always starts with a feeling of discomfort rather than a clear idea. Something in the field feels off to me. People are using a method, it works, everyone cites it, but when I actually try to explain to myself why it works, I can't. That gap between "it works" and "I understand why" is usually where I start.

ConvNeXt is a good example. Around 2021, Vision Transformers were taking over, and the narrative was that attention was the magic ingredient. But I kept asking: did we actually control for everything else? The training recipe, the augmentation, the architecture details that had nothing to do with attention? Nobody had done that experiment carefully. So the project began not as "let's build a new architecture," but as "let's be honest about what's actually driving the gains." The result came from the question, not the other way around.

The same thing happened with the representation work in diffusion models, with the REPA line. The discomfort there was that diffusion models were clearly learning something about images, but the internal representations seemed weirdly bad compared to self-supervised encoders. Why would a model that can generate photorealistic images not understand them well? That mismatch bothered me for a long time before it turned into a project.

So if I had to name the pattern: first, a nagging confusion that most people have agreed to ignore. Second, a very simple, almost embarrassingly simple experiment to test whether the confusion is real. I think young researchers underestimate how valuable the simple experiment is. You don't need a clever idea at the start. You need a clear question and the willingness to look at the result even if it tells you your hypothesis was wrong.

The third part, which I think is underrated, is patience with being wrong early. Many of these projects had several months where the results were messy or contradicted what I expected. The temptation is to drop it and move to something more fashionable. But the messy phase is usually where the real insight is hiding, because that's where the field's intuition and the evidence disagree.

And I'd add one more thing. The best early stages are collaborative in a loose way. I talk to students, I argue with colleagues, and often the question gets sharper because someone pushes back and says "that's obvious" or "that can't be true." Both reactions are useful. If everyone says it's obvious, I check whether anyone has actually verified it. If everyone says it can't be true, that's even more interesting.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting from discomfort or confusion and tolerating messy early results, but does not identify persistent failure to make things work at the outset as the recurring pattern.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it starts with a fairly simple question—something that feels a little inconsistent, or an assumption that everyone accepts but that I don’t fully understand. At that stage, I usually don’t know whether it will become a substantial research project. I just want to run a small experiment and see what happens.

Then, if the result is surprising, I keep digging. Often the interesting direction emerges from that process, rather than from having a big plan at the beginning. So the pattern is probably curiosity first, then small experiments, and gradually figuring out what the real question is.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting from a question or unclear assumption and trying a small experiment; it does not identify persistent failure to make things work at the outset as a recurring pattern.

sol-6.1.text: I think a lot of my best research starts with confusion. There’s something people take for granted, but I don’t quite understand why it should be true. So I spend time asking basic questions and trying simple experiments. Often the initial idea is wrong, but working through that confusion helps me find a better question. Looking back, the pattern is less about having a clear vision from the beginning and more about staying curious when something doesn’t make sense.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting with confusion, asking basic questions, and often having a wrong initial idea, but it does not identify persistent failure to make things work at the outset as a recurring pattern.
